title: A map as a matrix in a basis
objectives: Write a linear map as a matrix in chosen bases, and change basis.

screens.title: Differentiation as a table
screens.prose: $D : \mathcal{P}_3(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ sends each basis vector $1, x, x^2, x^3$ to the image shown. Write each image in coordinates of $(1, x, x^2)$, as a column. The rows are the coefficients of $1$, $x$ and $x^2$.
screens.question: Fill in each column.

hints.text: A column lists the coefficients of $1$, $x$, $x^2$ in one image.

feedback.correct: Right. Each column holds the coordinates of one image.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each image as $a + bx + cx^2$ and put $(a, b, c)$ down its column.

byKey.row: You put the 2 of $2x$ in the $x^2$ row. $2x$ is $2$ times $x$, so it goes in the $x$ row.
byKey.deg: You put the 3 of $3x^2$ in the $x$ row. It multiplies $x^2$, so it goes in the bottom row.

explain.text: $D1 = 0$ gives a zero column, and $Dx = 1$ puts a 1 in the top row. $Dx^2 = 2x$ and $Dx^3 = 3x^2$ fill the diagonal above. The table is the $3 \times 4$ matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&0\\0&0&2&0\\0&0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$.

screens.title: Where the basis goes
screens.prose: The sliders set the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}m_{11} & m_{12}\\ m_{21} & m_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ of $T$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$. It opens at l5's map. Move one slider at a time and watch the two arrows.
screens.question: Which entries does $T\mathbf{e}_1$ read?

hints.text: Move $m_{12}$ and watch which arrow moves.
$m_{12}$ moves $T\mathbf{e}_2$. So $T\mathbf{e}_1$ reads the other column.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move one slider at a time and see which arrow follows it.

explain.text: $m_{11}$ and $m_{21}$ move $T\mathbf{e}_1$, while $m_{12}$ and $m_{22}$ move $T\mathbf{e}_2$. So column $k$ of the matrix is the image of the $k$-th basis vector. That is the rule the hook used for $D$.

screens.title: The matrix of a map
screens.prose: Bases $\mathcal{B} = (\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $W$ give $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}^{\mathcal{C}}$: column $k$ is $[T\mathbf{v}_k]_{\mathcal{C}}$, the coordinates of $T\mathbf{v}_k$. One basis for an operator gives $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$. Take the shift $Sp(x) = p(x + 1)$ on $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ in $(1, x, x^2)$.
screens.question: What is $[S]$ in the basis $(1, x, x^2)$?

feedback.correct: Right. The columns are the coordinates of $1$, $1 + x$ and $1 + 2x + x^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shift each basis vector and write its coordinates as a column.

byKey.rows: You wrote the images as rows. That is the transpose; each image goes down a column.
byKey.length: The matrix of an operator on $\mathcal{P}_2$ is $3 \times 3$: one row and one column per basis vector.

explain.text: $Sx^2 = (x + 1)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2$, the solid curve, gives the third column $(1, 2, 1)$. With $S1 = 1$ and $Sx = 1 + x$ we get $\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&2\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Level 4 meets this $S$ again.

screens.title: Apply the matrix
screens.prose: Coordinates of $p = 3 + 2x + x^2$ are $[p] = (3, 2, 1)$. The matrix acts on coordinates: $[Sp] = [S][p]$.
screens.question: What is $[Sp]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each row of $[S]$ by $(3, 2, 1)$.

byKey.rows: You multiplied by the transpose of $[S]$. Each row of $[S]$ dots with $(3, 2, 1)$.
byKey.same: You left the coordinates unchanged. Multiply by $[S]$.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 3, one per coordinate.

explain.text: $[S](3, 2, 1) = (6, 4, 1)$, so $Sp = 6 + 4x + x^2$, as l5's quiz found by expanding. These are also l4's coordinates of $p$ in $(1, x - 1, (x - 1)^2)$. The matrix did the shift without any algebra.

screens.title: One map after another
screens.prose: $D \circ S$ first shifts $p \in \mathcal{P}_2$, then differentiates into $\mathcal{P}_1$. In bases $(1, x, x^2)$ and $(1, x)$, $[D]$ is $2 \times 3$ and $[S]$ is $3 \times 3$.
screens.question: Which matrix is $[D \circ S]$?

options.why: You wrote the maps in the order they act. The first map's matrix sits on the right, and $[S][D]$ is not even defined.
Composition is not addition, and the sizes differ.
That is the transpose of $[D][S]$, a $3 \times 2$ matrix.

hints.text: $[S]$ acts first, so it sits next to $[p]$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply $[S]$ to coordinates first, then $[D]$.

explain.text: $[D][S] = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&2\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$. Check the last column: $D((x + 1)^2) = 2x + 2$, coordinates $(2, 2)$. The matrix of a composition is the product, first map on the right.

screens.title: Rows or columns?
screens.prose: From l5, $T\mathbf{e}_1 = (2, 3)$ and $T\mathbf{e}_2 = (1, -2)$. A classmate writes these images as the rows of $[T]$.
screens.question: Which matrix is $[T]$ in the standard basis?

options.why: You wrote the images as rows. That is the transpose: it sends $\mathbf{e}_1$ to $(2, 1)$.
You swapped the columns. Column 1 must be $T\mathbf{e}_1$.

hints.text: Check: the matrix times $(1, 0)$ must give $(2, 3)$.

feedback.correct: Right. The images go down the columns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply each option by $(1, 0)$ and compare with $T\mathbf{e}_1$.

byKey.row: You wrote the images as rows. Times $(1, 0)$ that gives $(2, 1)$, not $T\mathbf{e}_1 = (2, 3)$.

explain.text: A matrix times $\mathbf{e}_1$ picks out its first column. So $T\mathbf{e}_1 = (2, 3)$ must be column 1. Writing images as rows gives the transpose, which is a different map.

screens.title: Why the matrix works
screens.prose: Prove $[T\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = [T]_{\mathcal{B}}^{\mathcal{C}}[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$, the rule we used on $p$. A matrix times a vector is the combination of its columns, weighted by the vector's entries.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Taking coordinates in $\mathcal{C}$ is linear, so $[T\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \sum c_k[T\mathbf{v}_k]_{\mathcal{C}}$.
Column $k$ of $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}^{\mathcal{C}}$ is $[T\mathbf{v}_k]_{\mathcal{C}}$, so this is $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}^{\mathcal{C}}[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: A column vector times a matrix has the wrong shape. The matrix acts on the vector from the left.

hints.text: Expand; apply $T$; coordinates; recognise the columns.

feedback.correct: Right. Linearity twice, then the column rule.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand, apply $T$, take coordinates, then read off the columns.

byKey.x1: You put the vector on the left. A matrix times a vector combines the matrix's columns.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: $T$ and the coordinate map are both linear, so $[T\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \sum c_k[T\mathbf{v}_k]_{\mathcal{C}}$. That is the combination of the columns with weights $c_k$. So the matrix does to coordinates what $T$ does to vectors.

screens.title: A better basis
screens.prose: Change of basis: $[T]_{\mathcal{B}'} = \mathbf{P}^{-1}[T]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbf{P}$, where $\mathbf{P}$'s columns are the new basis in old coordinates. Take `eigen` l13's $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1\\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and the new basis $\mathbf{x}_1 = (1, 1)$, $\mathbf{x}_2 = (1, -2)$. Each image stays on its line.
screens.question: What is the matrix of $\mathbf{A}$ in the basis $(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)$?

hints.text: Column 1 is the coordinates of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_1$ in the new basis.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each image in the new basis and use the column rule.

byKey.same: You kept the old matrix. In the new basis the columns are coordinates in $(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)$.
byKey.swap: You swapped the eigenvalues. Column 1 belongs to $\mathbf{x}_1$, and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_1 = 5\mathbf{x}_1$.
byKey.img: You wrote the images in old coordinates. In the new basis $(5, 5)$ is $5\mathbf{x}_1 + 0\mathbf{x}_2$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_1 = 5\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_2 = 2\mathbf{x}_2$, so the new coordinates are $(5, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$. That is $\mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} = \operatorname{diag}(5, 2)$, as in `eigen` l13. The same map, in a basis that suits it.

screens.title: Coordinates in the new grid
screens.prose: The grid is now drawn in the basis $\mathbf{b}_1 = (1, 1)$, $\mathbf{b}_2 = (1, -1)$. Count steps along the grid to reach the arrow.
screens.question: What is $[(5, 1)]$ in the basis $(\mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $a + b = 5$, $a - b = 1$.

byKey.std: You gave the standard coordinates. In this basis, count steps along $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$.
byKey.swap: You swapped the order. The first coordinate goes with $\mathbf{b}_1$.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 2, one per coordinate.

explain.text: $3(1, 1) + 2(1, -1) = (5, 1)$, so the coordinates are $(3, 2)$. The identity map from this basis to the standard one has matrix $\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, not $\mathbf{I}$. Solving $\mathbf{P}\mathbf{c} = (5, 1)$ is how the code finds coordinates.

screens.title: Change basis in code
screens.prose: A basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is given as the columns of `B`. Coordinates solve $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{v}$, and the matrix in the new basis is $\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$. Use `np.linalg.solve`, not an inverse. Columns of rank below $n$ are not a basis: raise `ValueError`.
screens.question: Complete `coords(v, B)` and `matrix_in_basis(A, B)`, rounding to 6 places.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def coords(v, B):
    # B's columns are a basis; raise ValueError
    # when they are not
    return v

def matrix_in_basis(A, B):
    # the matrix of A in the basis of B's columns
    return A
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Lists are compared exactly after rounding to 6 places, and two singular bases must raise `ValueError`. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: The new matrix: `np.linalg.solve(B, A @ B)`, which is $\mathbf{B}^{-1}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})$.
Check `np.linalg.matrix_rank(B) < n` first, then round with `np.round(..., 6) + 0.0` and return `.tolist()`.

feedback.correct: Right. Solving beats inverting, and rank decides what is a basis.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row: the new matrix, the coordinates, or the singular check?

byKey.test-1: In the eigenvector basis the matrix is $\operatorname{diag}(5, 2)$. Return `np.linalg.solve(B, A @ B)`.
byKey.test-7: The columns $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 4)$ are parallel. Check `matrix_rank(B) < n` and raise `ValueError`.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check the shapes you pass to `solve`.

explain.text:
`solve(B, A @ B)` computes $\mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$ without forming an inverse. The shift's matrix in $(1, 1 + x, 1 + x + x^2)$ came out as $\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&2\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$. A rank test catches the singular basis before `solve` does.

```python
M = np.linalg.solve(B, A @ B)
```

screens.title: Market and spread
screens.prose: Two stocks have daily covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, in $\%^2$. In the basis "market" $(1, 1)$ and "spread" $(1, -1)$, the operator $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ becomes $\operatorname{diag}(4, 2)$. A variance is a quadratic form, $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$.
screens.question: What is the variance of the market portfolio $\mathbf{w} = (1, 1)$, in $\%^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{w}$: all four entries of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ count.

byKey.op: You read the operator's entry 4. $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ sends $(1, 1)$ to $4(1, 1)$, but the variance is $(1, 1) \cdot (4, 4) = 8$.
byKey.diag: You added the two variances and dropped the covariance. It counts twice: $3 + 3 + 2 \times 1$.

explain.text: $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}(1, 1) = (4, 4)$, and $(1, 1) \cdot (4, 4) = 8$. As a quadratic form, $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$ changes by $\mathbf{P}^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{P} = \operatorname{diag}(8, 4)$, not by $\mathbf{P}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{P}$. The two agree when $\mathbf{P}$ is orthonormal, which level 4 exploits.

The matrix of a composition is the product, with the first map on the right.
Changing basis gives $\mathbf{P}^{-1}[T]\mathbf{P}$, where $\mathbf{P}$'s columns are the new basis in old coordinates.

formula.name: Change of basis
formula.note: Read right to left: into old coordinates, apply $T$, back to new.

summary.trap: Images go down the columns. Written as rows they give the transpose, a different map.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{P}$'s columns are a new basis in old coordinates, so $\mathbf{P}$ turns new coordinates into old ones. $[T]$ is the matrix in the old basis.
quiz.question: Which matrix acts on new coordinates?

options.why: That converts the wrong way. It would act on old coordinates, using a matrix known in the new basis.
Its output is still in old coordinates. Convert back with $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.
Its input must be old coordinates. Convert the input with $\mathbf{P}$ first.

feedback.correct: Right. Convert in with $\mathbf{P}$, apply $[T]$, convert out with $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the product from right to left, starting from new coordinates.

explain.text: Read right to left: $\mathbf{P}$ turns new coordinates into old, $[T]$ acts, and $\mathbf{P}^{-1}$ turns the result back. So $[T]_{\mathcal{B}'} = \mathbf{P}^{-1}[T]\mathbf{P}$. With `eigen` l13's numbers it gave $\operatorname{diag}(5, 2)$.

quiz.prose: Let $\mathcal{B} = ((1, 1), (1, -1))$ and $\mathcal{E}$ the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$. $I$ is the identity map.
quiz.question: What is $[I]_{\mathcal{B}}^{\mathcal{E}}$?

options.why: That is $[I]$ with one basis on both sides. Here the bases differ.

feedback.correct: Right. Column $k$ is $I\mathbf{b}_k = \mathbf{b}_k$ in standard coordinates.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the column rule: column $k$ is $[I\mathbf{b}_k]_{\mathcal{E}}$.

explain.text: $I\mathbf{b}_1 = (1, 1)$ and $I\mathbf{b}_2 = (1, -1)$, written in the standard basis. So the identity map has matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the change-of-basis matrix. Only one basis on both sides gives $\mathbf{I}$.

quiz.question: What is $[T]$ in the standard basis?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $T\mathbf{e}_1$ and $T\mathbf{e}_2$ and use them as columns.

byKey.rows: You wrote the images as rows. $T\mathbf{e}_1 = (1, 0)$ goes down the first column.

explain.text: $T(1, 0) = (1, 0)$ and $T(0, 1) = (2, 3)$. As columns they give $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. Its rows are the coefficients of the formula, which is a quick check.

quiz.prose: $D : \mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}) \to \mathcal{P}_1(\mathbb{R})$, in the bases $(1, x, x^2)$ and $(1, x)$.
quiz.question: What is $[D]$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $D1$, $Dx$, $Dx^2$ in the basis $(1, x)$.

byKey.sq: You used $\mathcal{P}_2$ for the outputs too. The codomain $\mathcal{P}_1$ has dimension 2, so there are 2 rows.
byKey.length: A map from a space of dimension 3 to one of dimension 2 has a $2 \times 3$ matrix.

explain.text: $D1 = 0$, $Dx = 1$ and $Dx^2 = 2x$ have coordinates $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$ in $(1, x)$. So $[D]$ is $2 \times 3$. Rows count the codomain's dimension and columns the domain's.
